# Suvaṇṇakakkaṭajātaka (Ja 389)

**ID:** Ja 389
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Suvaṇṇakakkaṭajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul5.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Suvaṇṇakakkaṭajātaka* (Ja 389), known in English as *The Golden Crab*, is a tale preserved in the canonical Jātaka collection. According to the narrative frame, the Buddha told this birth-story while residing at the Bamboo Grove (*Veḷuvana*) to commemorate the Elder Ānanda offering up his life for the Buddha's sake when confronted by the elephant Dhanapāla. When the monks in the Hall of Truth discussed Ānanda’s self-sacrifice, the Buddha stated that Ānanda had also given up his life for him in past births, introducing the story with the opening words "Gold-clawed creature". The core narrative involves the Bodhisatta carrying a golden crab (*suvaṇṇakakkaṭaka* / *kañcanakakkaṭaka*) that comes to his aid against a snake and a crow [Fausböll 1883].

Outside of textual transmission, episodes of the *Suvaṇṇakakkaṭajātaka* are known in Southeast Asian art and epigraphy, having been documented on Buddhist boundary markers (*sīmā* / *semā* stones) from the Khorat Plateau and Chi Valley culture in Northeast Thailand [Murphy; Skilling].

**Sources**

- [Fausböll 1883] V. Fausböll, Jataka Together with Its Commentary, Vol. 3 (1883) — Provided the Pali prose details mentioning the Bodhisatta, the golden crab, snake, and crow.
- [Murphy] Stephen A. Murphy, Buddhist Boundary Markers of Northeast Thailand and Central Laos, 7th-12th C…Khorat Plateau — Attested the representation of the Suvaṇṇakakkaṭa Jātaka on Khorat Plateau Buddhist boundary stones and in the Phimai Museum.
- [Skilling] Peter Skilling, Jātaka and Paññāsa-jātaka in South-East Asia — Noted scholarship on the Suvaṇṇakakkaṭa-Jātaka depicted on sema stones in the Chi Valley culture.
